QF.id: AIFM CII Legal Documents and Negotiations_30

question.text: 'Konkan Credit Opportunities II AIF' is negotiating its distribution waterfall. LP 'Surya Sovereign Fund' demands a robust GP clawback. Which of the following is the PRIMARY economic purpose of a GP clawback provision in a Cat II AIF?

answer.text: To force the GP to return management fees that exceed 2% per annum.

To recapture carried interest previously paid to the GP if subsequent losses or a final-close whole-fund reconciliation show that the GP was overpaid relative to the agreed preferred-return / catch-up / split formula.
To claw back the GP commitment itself if the fund fails to achieve the hurdle rate.
To require the GP to reimburse LPs for any regulatory fine imposed by SEBI.

explanation.text: The Logic: A GP clawback exists to ensure that across the LIFE OF THE FUND, the GP does not end up retaining more carried interest than what the agreed waterfall formula (preferred return + catch-up + 80/20 split) entitles it to. Early deal-by-deal distributions can overpay the GP if later investments underperform; clawback recaptures that excess at fund-end. It does NOT touch management fees, GP commit, or regulatory fines — those are handled elsewhere in the LPA. The Trap: Management-fee cap is separate (and 2%/year is not a universal limit). GP commitment is skin-in-the-game capital, not clawback-able. Regulatory-fine reimbursement is a separate indemnity/liability construct. Cross-Exam Context: XIX-C covers clawback identically. XIX-B Cat III Distributor exam focuses more on HWM-reset mechanics — which is Cat III and NOT tested at Cat I/II level. Manager's Pro-Tip: Insist on clawback being secured — either through an escrow (typically 20-30% of carry held back) or a personal GP guarantee from senior partners. An unsecured clawback against a now-defunct GP entity at fund end is economically worthless.
